variants.headline: Ordered goods reach the dock
variants.sub: Imported {good} ordered by {company} has landed at the colony's port.
variants.body:
The company {company} has received {qty} units of {good} at the port. The order arrived a full round trip after it was placed and was paid for on the dock. For {target}, the event is a practical test of the connection between ordering, waiting and obtaining goods.

The sequence matters: an order, a full round trip, then delivery and payment on the dock. Stock received is different from stock expected. Managers should assess the timing of procurement with that distinction in mind, rather than confuse a placed order with a supply already available for use.

We favour {target} in this assessment. Goods actually landed and paid for deserve recognition as practical provision, even while the long route remains an essential part of any fair account of the achievement. Reliable assessment begins with particulars rather than a politically convenient assumption.

variants.headline: An order completes its long journey
variants.sub: The company {company} has taken delivery of its home-world order of {good}.
variants.body:

variants.headline: Imports landed and paid for
variants.sub: The company {company} has received its imported order of {good} at the port.
variants.body:
